2.	Does the Government intend to give effect to this legislation?
3.	What action, if any, has the Government taken to assist the Imperial Government in bringing about Government control of ocean carriers doing business (or from time to time doing business) between ports in the United Kingdom and ports in the Dominion of Canada?

The recommendations referred to have been considered by the Government and the subject matter discussed with other Overseas Premiers and the Premier of Great Britain. An Imperial Shipping Committee was appointed by the British Government in June, 1920, to inquire into and report on all matters connected with ocean freights and facilities and on all matters connected with the development and improvement of sea communications between the different parts of the Empire. On this committee Canada and other Overseas Dominions are represented. This committee has been in session and a preliminary report has been made on ship-owners' liabilities under bills of lading and matters pertaining thereto. This will doubtless be followed by reports on other phases of the subject being investigated by the above-named committee. After this investigation is finished and the reports made, what action, if any, is to be taken by the Government will have to be

determined after the reception and consideration of these reports of the committee.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my
intention to make any extended remarks in regard to the Budget which the Min-

ister of Finance has brought down. In a general way I would like to observe that the Budget, as I see it, is not going to bring any relief to the great consuming masses of the people of this country but will place additional burdens on their backs. I had hoped that the Government would have undertaken some revision of the tariff which would have resulted in a reduction of the taxation levied on the necessities of life, which cost so large a proportion of the income, not only of the labouring and farming classes, but also of those who form what may be called the middle classes of society. However, we have been disappointed in this regard notwithstanding the many promises made throughout the country by the Government and its supporters.
Permit me to say that we are faced at the present time with a very difficult situation indeed, and one which is bound to have a very prejudicial affect upon the country, more particularly in the matter of agricultural production. It is not my intention to review at great length the events of 1911, but I think it is recognized to-day -not only by this House but by the people generally-that had the reciprocity pact of that year been accepted by this country it would have been one of the greatest booms that Canada ever enjoyed. That has been proved, to some extent, by the action of the Government itself, which, although it helped to repudiate reciprocity in 1911, subsequently adopted some of its important provisions. The removal by the United States of the duties on cattle, sheep and hogs, resulted in the live stock 'industry in this country making very great strides. In the western part of the province of Ontario the cattle, sheep and hog industry was greatly helped by the taking down of the tariff barriers; but the prospect of a reimposition of those duties has caused in the minds of our farmers a feeling of perturbation; they do not know exactly where they are going to find markets if the tariff barriers are raised again, and they are most anxious that they should continue to enjoy the benefits which they have experienced partially but which they would have had in toto had the reciprocity agreement been accepted by Canada. I hope it is not too late for measures to be taken looking to that end. What is proposed at Washington is only a temporary tariff, and it would be well to enter into negotiations with the Government there to see whether some arrangement cannot be entered into whereby we might have trade relations which would be to the benefit of both coun-
tries. I do not mean by that that we should go hat in hand and ask in a pleading or humiliating way for concessions on the part of the United States administration. But we have things they want and they have things which we need, and if we can enter into any arrangement for commercial intercourse on mutually advantageous terms, it would be of the greatest possible benefit to the live stock industry of this country. As I say, the Fordney Bill is only a temporary measure. These two countries are peculiarly situated, they are neighbours for three or four thousand miles, and it is to be hoped that their longstanding friendly relations will never be interrupted. So I think the time is probably overripe-it is ripe, anyway-for the Government to take some action with a view to restoring to our cattle raisers the benefits of the American market which they have hitherto enjoyed.
If the Government do not think well to take such action, they must provide another outlet for our cattle, and I would suggest to the Prime Minister that during his visit to the Old Country-and I wish him all good fortune in the undertaking- he should attempt in a reasonable businesslike way, without meddling in their domestic affairs, to impress upon the British Government the mutual benefit of doing away with the embargo on our cattle. The matter has already been taken up with the. British authorities, but coming from the Prime Minister the prestige of his position would give added weight to his representations, and I am sure he would succeed in inducing the British people to see that justice is done to our cattle raisers. There can be no doubt that the so-called facts which induced the British Government to impose that embargo do not now, and in fact never did, exist, and its removal would confer a two-fold benefit, it would provide an outlet for our cattle, and at the same time it would enable the British people to get cheaper meat.
This debate, Mr. Speaker, has wandered pretty far afield, but throughout its course I have noticed that the Government seem to be very much bothered about us on this side of the House. Even the Prime Minister thinks we are getting into difficulties, and he would like to make it appear that we and our friends to the left are about to enter into an unholy alliance, and are intent on taking down the tariff barriers that now surround the country. He charges us with inconsistency and, in common with some of his supporters, seems to

be very solicitous in regard to the attitude which my hon. friend's on this side have taken. He seems so very solicitous that really I cannot understand his anxiety. He is bothered about the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) and is afraid that he will not retain his seat. That is a rather kindly solicitude coming from the Prime Minister for an hon. member who is opposed to him.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Crocodile tears.

subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, crocodile tears. He seems to be bothered about my hon. friend from Montreal (Mr. Rinfret) also, and about my hon. friend from West Peterborough (Mr. Gordon). He seems to think that we are not sincere, and he presumes to admonish us in regard to our sincerity and consistency. With all respect to the right hon. gentleman, I would tell him that it would be well for him to scrutinize some of his own supporters. He would probably find then that he had his hands full, and he might have some tremors as to just what line some of them would take on a protection motion. For my own part, I do not see how my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Henders) can, consistently stick to the Prime Minister on this occasion; nor can I see how my hon. friend from Swift Current (Mr. Argue) can follow the Prime Minister in view of the statements he has made in times past as to the trade policy that this country should adopt; nor do I see how my hon. and gallant friend from Skeena (Mr. Peck) can support the Prime Minister, if he is to be consistent with former declarations made on the platform and in this House. But I may come closer to the Prime Minister, to members of his own cabinet. I have very grave doubts-rather I have not any doubts-if he wishes to be consistent, in regard to the attitude of the Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Guthrie) on this amendment.
The right hon. Prime Minister last week made a very long and clever speech, but it was not the best that I have heard him deliver in this House. At times I was surprised at his lack of logic, remembering his peculiarly subtle mind, and it seemed to me that he forgot that vituperation is not argument, nor is declamation logic. There is a principle in the British constitution that there should be solidarity in the cabinet, and, looking at the past history of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence, I really cannot see how he can refuse to support the amendment moved by the hon.
member for Shelburne and Queen's. It is only seven short years ago that he was one in the fighting phalanx on this side of the House. He carried the banner of Liberalism particularly high, and especially the banner of tariff reform as espoused (by the Liberal party in this House and in the country. I have heard him on more than one occasion declaiming for the benefits of free agricultural implements, for a lower tariff all round, for assistance to the great consuming masses, and I have heard him rail at the Manufacturers' Association in no uncertain tones. But now the scene is changed. The attainment of power and his new environment seem to have made him another man. Contrasting his political past with his political present he seems to be a sort of political Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde in regard to the tariff policy. Not so very long ago he indulged in this House in quite a tirade against my hon. friends to my left. And in passing I would like to compliment their leader, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) on his speech of yesterday, which I think is one of the best I have ever heard in this House. The Minister of Militia was gibing the farmers with not being loyal to the industries of this country, and consequently, I presume, not loyal to Canada herself. He intimated that they did not want to buy Canadian made goods, but prefered American, and he thought that was an outrageous policy for them to pursue. Now, what has been the policy of the Minister of Militia? As long as I have known him, until this sudden change, he had been a consistent supporter of the principles of the Liberal party. Let us look at his political history for a few moments, and while in doing this I may be adding to the material which has already been put on Hansard by the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee), I think it well to do so, to show just how far there can be solidarity in this cabinet in regard to tariff policy. The Minister of Militia, speaking in this House on March 1st, as reported on page 443 of Hansard, used this language:
But what is this organization doing? What is the party supported by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) doing to-day? Look at the millions upon millions of dollars that are going out of this country every year-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I must point out to the hon. member that it is a part of the unwritten law of parliament that a member, in speaking, cannot refer to anything said or done in a previous debate

BK<	_
during the same session and that he is not in order in quoting from a previous debate.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I bow
to your ruling. But I may point out that the hon. minister, after indulging in this tirade against the farmers, intimated that the removal of the duty on farm implements would result in the destruction of all implement manufacturing industries in this country, and that it would make valueless all the capital invested in them. He said that the manufacturers would lose everything they had put into those industries; that the Americans would come here and steal our market; that Canadian labour would not be used, and that our money would be spent in buying American goods. I am sorry that I cannot quote his exact words, but I think that is just about what he said; I am sure he will not deny it. Now, in March, 1914, a motion was made by Mr. Knowles, then a member of the House, to put agricultural implements on the free list, and in the course of the debate on that motion the Minister of Militia made another very positive speech. He generally makes positive speeches and sometimes issues challenges to hon. gentlemen holding different views; in this case his remarks were just as positive as usual. To-day he is absolutely opposed to the admission of agricultural implements free of duty, on the ground that it would be unpatriotic. Well, I do not see anything in the condition of the country at the present time to make any difference between what would be unpatriotic now and what was unpatriotic in 1914. Here is what the present Minister of Militia said in 1914:
There is only one thing left for him to do-
Referring to the Prime Minister.
-and that is to reduce the tariff on agricultural implements to a minimum. In my view, that will not toe as satisfactory as the complete abolition of the duties upon agricultural implements. But from the statement of the Prime Minister at six o'clock, his followers from the western provinces who represent agricultural constituencies, and his followers from the province of Ontario who represent the Wellingtons, the Dufferins, the Oxfords and the Waterloos, can tell their constituents that the great boon of free agricultural implements has been denied to them this day by the Prime Minister of Canada, who is the mouthpiece of the Government.
These were the words used by the present Minister of Militia on March 11, 1914, in this House. At that time he was not Minister of Militia; he was the great tribune of the people. He went on to say:
[The Deputy Speaker.]
I rose on this occasion chiefly because I think that some member from the province of Ontario should interject some remarks into this debate to show that the demand for agricultural implements is by no means limited to the western provinces of Canada. The riding which I have the honour to represent in this House is about equally made up of urban and of rural inhabitants. I am satisfied that, irrespective of party, the people engaged in agriculture in the county of Wellington, north or south, would hold up both hands for the boon of free agricultural implements.
When my hon. friend goes back to his constituency some time in the course of a year or two, what will the people of North and South Wellington say to him in regard to this volte-face in the matter of free agricultural implements-a condition necessary to the proper carrying on of agricultural work by his farmer friends? The hon. gentleman went on to say:
From the Atlantic to the Pacific, the demand is as broad as is the country. I then ask the Government: Why not accede to a demand of that kind when your revenue is going to suffer so little and when no Canadian industry is going to be injured?
In 1914 the hon. gentleman referred to this question as a very grave one. In 1921, speaking on this very same "grave question," he contends in all seriousness that if we have free agricultural implements all the agricultural implement industries of this country will he wiped out. In 1914 he said:
I then ask the Government: Why not accede to a demand of that kind when your revenue is going- to suffer so little and when no Canadian industry is going to be injured?
The hon. gentleman at that time was [DOT] even more ardent in his support of the motion than its sponsor, Mr. Knowles. It is generally understood that agricultural implements cover only such articles as mowers, reapers, and a few other things; their number is not large so far as the tariff schedules are concerned. But in 1914, in the speech to which I have been referring, the hon. gentleman went on to say:
I,	for one, believe that of all the industries in Canada the agricultural implement industry is the one now best able to stand without the support of any customs tariff at all. I made a little list of twenty-five articles which are generally and properly considered agricultural implements.
I know that some hon. members in referring to agricultural implements include only reapers, mowers, binders and a few other articles, but T cannot see why the list should not be much more extended.
So the hon. gentleman at that time wanted to extend the application of the

Sb3E>
term "agricultural implements" to some twenty-five different articles and have them all made free of duty. He promised to give a list of these articles in response to a question put by Mr. Sharpe, but I do not see that the list was ever given. So there we have some of the history of the hon. gentleman so far as his stand on this ''ery important question of agricultural implements is concerned.
But that was not the latest stand which he took on the subject prior to this year. Even as late as 1917 his conversion had not been effected; he was still in favour of free agricultural implements. In 1917 a motion was moved in this House by Hon. Frank Oliver, of which the following is a part:	-
That in the opinion of this House it would he in the public interest if the Customs Tariff Act were so amended as to provide:
1.	That wheat, wheat flour, and all other products of wheat be placed upon the free list
2.	That farm implements and machinery, farm tractors, mining, flour and saw-mill machinery, and repairs for same, rough and partly dressed lumber, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils, cement and fertilizers be added to the free list.
The hon. Minister of Militia expressed his approval of that policy. There seems, therefore, to be a good deal of inconsistency and' considerable lack of harmony on the tariff question, even among the followers of my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen). He had better look after his own house and not bother about hon. gentlemen on this side
As I have said, the Minister of Militia has always been one of the greatest opponents in this House of the principle of protection. We can find this out by looking through the old debates-and they are very interesting-when the minister makes statements in regard to the tariff policy of this country. He says to-day-at least I presume he does, because I suppose he is following his leader, as this is a very important matter and the Cabinet should be of one mind in regard to it-that he and his Government are in favour of the principle of protection. That is not what he used to say. In the olden days, if I remember aright, the Minister of Militia was in favour of a revenue tariff, but to-day he is going further; he wants to help the privileged classes; he is more closely associated with the Manufacturers' Association or, at any rate, more friendly to them, and he has abandoned those clients and friends of his of the olden days, the great consuming masses and the farmers of his riding.
What did he say in 1911-12 in regard to
2241	[	'
this question. At that time there was before the House a very important measure, introduced, I think, by the then Prime Minister, to establish a permanent tariff commission in this country. The present Minister of Militia was not in favour of that measure, and on the second reading of the Bill providing for the establishment of a permanent tariff commission the minister made certain observations. I want to dwell upon this point because it shows such a complete change of heart on the part of the minister. All through these speeches of his he has been referring to the burden that the tariff will place on the great consuming masses, on labour and so on, but to-day he seems to have forgotten these people entirely. At page 2602 of Volume II of Hansard of 1911-12, the present Minister of Militia spoke as follows:
But apart from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, has any call come from any other section of the country?
That is, for the appointment of a permanent tariff commission.
I ask my hon. friend the Minister of FSnanc4: Have any agricultural societies in Canada asked for the establishment of a permanent tariff commission? Have any of the dairymen's associations-*
In those days he was looking after the different associations connected with agriculture and the raising of live stock.
-any of the live stock associations, swine breeders' or sheep breeders' associations, any western associations, the Grain Growers' Association, the Dominion Grange-have any of these men asked for it? Have any of the great consuming classes asked for such a measure?
That was the position of the Minister of Militia in 1911-12. He was the protector of the consuming masses, of the grain growers, the sheep breeders, the swine breeders, and he had a little soft spot in his heart even for his present enemies across the way. That was not all that he said at that time. At page 2603 of the same volume of Hansard he used these words:
It does, Sir, seem to me a strange thing that the first important official act, the first act, at all events, of any consequence or any magnitude, performed by the Minister of Finance in this House since his appointment to that high position a few monthes ago, should be the introduction of a Bill to establish a permanent tariff commission in Canada, a Bill which, on his own statement, both in form and in substance, I think I am safe in saying, is practically borrowed from the highest protectionist country in the world, from the United States of America. It is a strange comment, a strange sequel, upon events which happened just about a year ago in Massey Hall, Toronto, at a tremendous gathering called by so-called Liberals to protest

against the proposed reciprocity agreement with the United States.
They were "so-called Liberals" because they did not believe in reciprocity. I suppose, as regards others who believed in those days in reciprocity, in greater freedom of trade, free farm implements and a number of other things, and who do not do so now, it would not be kind to call them "so-called Liberals"-they have become hard-shell Tories, pure and simple. A little further on the minister went on to say, speaking of the Minister of Finance of that day:
He will remember, as I do, that one member of the House of Representatives said: I support this Bill because it is the best way to sustain the glorious doctrine of protection.
Thus showing that he himself was bitterly opposed to that "glorious doctrine" of protection, which he is espousing so bravely and loyally to-day. A little further on he used these words:
A tariff commission board seems to be a necessary adjunct to the high protective system, and I do not think I am going one jot beyond the truth when I say that this Bill is brought in here

almost the first important Bill of the first session of this Parliament- as a quid pro quo for the Canadian Manufacturers' Association to redeem the promises made to them for their generous and lavish support during the election on September 21 last.
I wonder if one can apply those words to-day. I wonder if this stand as regards protection is not another bid from hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of the House to get the Canadian manufacturers and the big interests of this country to back them again as they did in 1911, and by misrepresentations about various things sweep them again into power. It looks very much as if this were a duplication of their effort of 1911; but I prophesy that you cannot fool the people all the time, and failure will confront my hon. friends whenever the election day comes. A little further on the hon. gentleman used these words:
Is that not plain enough? Do the people not believe that the Government's proposal means that the Board of Tariff Commissioners shall, from time to time, make reports upon which this Government will act, and that these reports, in the very nature of things, will be in the interest of higher duties or greater protection to the industries of Canada,-or, in the words of the Prime Minister, will be designed to give the industries of Canada more than a fair chance? If they give them more than a fair chance, somebody is going to suffer. It is at the expense of somebody else.
At whose expense is it to be? Certainly, at the expense of the great consuming masses of this country.

That is a clear admission that, by the Government's adherence to a policy of protection, to which at that time my hon. friend did not adhere, the great masses of the people were going to be injured. A little further on he made use of - these words:
The fact, therefore, is that we are going to have three permanent tariff commissioners, a board just as permanently appointed as a bench of judges is appointed; and that the qualification is that they shall be loyal subjects and followers of the right hon. gentleman who is now Prime Minister of Canada. They are to be Conservatives first, last, and all the time, and if they are, they have also got to be protectionists and high protectionists. We may make up our minds to it that we are going to have a board made up of individuals who rightly or wrongly hold opinions in favour of a highly protective system in this Dominion.
Mr. Blain:	Is not my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) a protectionist himself?
Mr. Guthrie: I believe in a certain amount of protection ; a tariff for revenue. A tariff for revenue affords enough protection in my community and in my opinion it is sufficient.
Later on, in the course of that address, the hon. member spoke of his being in favour of a revenue tariff. Consequently, as late as 1912, my hon. friend was not in favour of the protective principle except as far as there was incidental protection in a revenue tariff. Further on he says:
My own opinion is that, while it may fall somewhat short of the ideal of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, it is a perfect "lemon" for the farmers and workers of Canada.
That is the establishment of a tariff commission which meant "protection" as he said.
They will be fooled and hoodwinked by such a measure. They have a right, I believe, to look for better treatment at the hands of the right hon. Prime Minister.
The hon. member then moved the six months' hoist. All this was a struggle to prevent protection from becoming a factor in the tariff policy of this country. The whole political policy of the Minister of Militia up to a session or so ago when he joined this Government, has been to tear down the tariff walls around this country and make trade freer. But a wonderful change has come over the hon. gentleman since he entered this Government and became Minister of Militia.
Just at this point I would like to touch on some criticisms that the Minister of Militia has made on the attitude we on this side of the House have taken with regard to certain of his Estimates. My hon. friend from Kent (Mr. MeCoig)

3537 moved that the vote of $1,500,000 in the minister's Estimates for annual drill should be cut in two. The Minister of Militia took great exception to that, and in a very eloquent peroration tried to leave the impression on the country that we on this side of the House were not friendly to the boys in the trenches, but were endeavouring to make them do their duty twice; it was suggested that we had not their interests at heart. Now I presume it is known to this House and to the country that just as many Liberals and sons of Liberals died on the fields of France and Flanders as Conservatives and the sons of Conservatives. The suggestion that was made from this side of the House to cut that vote in two was made solely in the interests of economy. It was a good suggestion, and I heartily approved of it. I think the minister's argument on that occasion destroyed itself, because he said: Unless we do the thing properly, we might as well save the money. Now, if any boy can get much benefit by taking six days' drill, I will have to be shown something more than I know at present of the drills that have taken place in this country from year to year.
But that is not altogether the point. Our argument was this: In 1921 Canada is in a different position from what she has been in for many a year. The war is over; peace is established, and, we believe, firmly established. Not so very long ago I had the pleasure of listening to one of the Prime Ministers of the greatest selfgoverning dominions, and he said that he did not believe we would have another war in this generation. So we have come back to a peace basis, and we do not need to be looking for trouble and spending money on military matters to the extent we did in the past. It is not as if we were in Europe, with an armed camp all around us. We are isolated here in Canada. We are not unfriendly with the country to the south of us. We are a peaceable people, and we desire peace, and on grounds of economy alone, if for no other reason, I believe it would be wise for us to save this money we are expending on military matters, and use it for expanding our trade, and in other more profitable ways that will readily suggest themselves to the minds of all hon. members.
What attitude did the present Minister of Militia take in regard to a similar vote in this House in 1914? The Minister of Militia of that day, now the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) had an
item in his Estimates of $2,000,000 for annual training. My hon. friend the present Minister of Militia seemed at that time to be the critic of militia Estimates, and he was very much in favour of reducing this item of $2,000,000 for military training; so much so, that he thought it would be a good argument to back up his position by referring to the past record of the gentlemen with whom he is now associated, and he went back to the time when my hon. friend who is now Minister of Trade and Commerce Sir George Foster) was Minister of Finance, and pointed out what he did under similar circumstances. Then he went on to advocate that military drill should be cut out on grounds of economy. I will give you his exact words:
On their face these Estimates are wrong. There is a statement that there is less spent this year than last. I remember in the old days of the Conservative party, prior to 1896. That was a year very much like this. There was a falling revenue and an increasing expenditure. Times were hard and unemployment was general throughout the land. How did the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) who was then Minister of Finance, face the situation? Did he increase the military expenditure? No. he did not send the men out to drill that year and he saved between $600,000 and $700,000 to the people of Canada 'by one stroke of the pen. A similar situation confronts us to-day-a falling revenue, a rising expenditure and the militia expenditure, of all others, rising faster in proportion than the expenditure of any other department of the Government.
Further on he said:
Look at the other requirements of Canada calling for our attention to-day.
I contend that here we have an absolute confirmation of the rightfulness of the position we have taken with regard to the proposed expenditure on drill. The conditions are even worse to-day; our revenues are falling, hard times are upon us, unemployment is general throughout the country; and if there is one thing that this Government needs to study at the present time it is economy. I submit that the position taken by the Minister of Militia in this House this session with regard to this item for drill was absolutely out of accord with the position he took in 1914.
In the year 1912 also the present Minister of Militia was desirous of reducing other military Estimates. He even went so far, as you will see by page 6452, Volume 4, of the Debates of 1912-13, as to say in reply to the suggestion of the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) for a naval holiday:
Yes, and take a holiday in naval matters, and go forward with this Bank Act and-the private

legislation and the other pressing measures which are before the country and which have been held up by the Government.
So in those days when my hon. friend was on this side of the House he was a great champion of reduction in military expenditures. I say that our attitude is much more justified at this time by the situation in which this country finds itself to-day.
I shall not detain the House much longer, as I have already spoken longer than I had intended. There is just one thing further that I wish to say. There seems to be on the other side of the House a great deal of fear among many hon. members who have spoken as to the attitude of hon. members of the Progressive party. That fear seems to pervade the mind and heart not only of the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) but of the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Cowan), the hon. member for Prontenac (Mr. Edwards) and quite a few other hon. gentlemen opposite. There seems to be some suspicion in their minds that the Progressive elements in this country might form an alliance; that our friends to my left at some time in the future, either before or after the election, might join with us in endeavouring to give good government to this country. I do not know that that is such a horrible prospect to contemplate. I do not know that such an alliance would strike terror into the hearts of the people. I do not know but that worse things might happen to this country. Which would be the better for this country-a union or alliance of the moderating wisdom of experienced Liberalism with the progressive ideals of ardent and advanced agrarianism, or an alliance of decrepit, decayed, and moribund Toryism with the selfish, reactionary ideals of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association? It seems to me that the former are pretty vigorous parents, and that they would breed a pretty sound offspring. I think that they would do in Canada what was done in 1896; they would bring prosperity, progress and contentment to the masses of the people, and they would bring flourishing industries into Canada and make this country a great nation. On the other hand, our friends opposite, by the alliance which apparently they desire to make, could only bring forth an offspring that would mean a continuation of special privilege in this country and that would not make for the contentment of the masses, but would rather, on the contrary, impose upon them, in the future, the taxation they have had to bear in the past. friends, by that alliance, would do nothing to promote flourishing business; they would simply bring stagnation to business and trade, and instead of building up a great nation, they would help to reduce this promising country to the stature of a dwarf nation. I do not care whether or not this alliance is consummated between the Agrarians and this party; but I do say, Mr. Speaker, that after the next Parliament, it is my belief that either a union of these two great vitalizing elements in this country will go forward to carry out the policy enunciated in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), or, if they do not unite to prosecute that policy, then there will be in Parliament either an Agrarian party, or a Liberal party which will carry out this policy and build up the country, making it more happy and prosperous than it is at present, or than it could otherwise hope to be.

I did not expect that I should be called upon so suddenly to take part in the debate. I had not thought it possible that I should . have to follow immediately an hon. member on this side of the House; I had no idea that our friends across the way had contemplated so early a surrender. My reason for not contributing to the debate at an earlier stage is the fact that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), one of the twelve members representing the people of Alberta in this House, is usually accorded the right to precede those members in an important debate such as this, in view of his eloquence and his knowledge of economic affairs. I had been waiting for some hon. member from my province to get up and in some measure endeavour to make an argument against the views advanced by the hon. member for Red Deer, but so far not one of them has accepted the challenge.
We know, Mr. Speaker, that in Canada to-day things are not what they were a few years ago; things are on the retrograde rather than progressive 4 p.m. in Alberta, as in other parts of the Dominion. But one would imagine, from the silence of the representatives of that province, that we were back in the year 1896 when there was only one representative for the whole province of Alberta-although, let me say, he was some representative. Nothing ever transpired in reference to his province on which he did not have something to say; I suppose it is hardly necessary for me to state that I refer to Hon. Frank Oliver. But

Mr. Speaker, I do not know that even at that time, away back in 1896, we were not about as well represented in Parliament as we have ever been since. We had then one energetic and active man to take care of our interests. If things were in a prosperous state, or if we had some reasonable ground for hope that conditions would be bettered by the administration of this Government we could excuse the inactivity of hon. gentlemen who sit behind them. I may say, in passing, that I am a pretty old resident of that province, having spent some forty years there, and during all that time-and my experineces were father hard in the early eighties-I do not believe that the people ever had to struggle as hard to make ends meet as at the present [DOT] time. It was surprising to those who came at a later date and were able to prosper in that province to be told of the hard times which we had experienced in the old days; they thought we were telling them a -tale in which there was more romance than truth. But they are beginning to realize, as We did, what real hard times mean, and what it is to have a Tory Government in power. Hon. gentlemen opposite may say that difficult conditions to-day are not peculiar to Canada, but are world-wide; but I contend that with a proper government we should still be able to carry on. The Government has tampered With everything. They have tampered with the administration of lands., tampered with the regulations in regard to oils, tampered with the development of our country, and tampered with the oil and mining leases, until to-day no investor has courage enough to come in and take a chance. Day after day I have received letters of complaint from various classes of people; sometimes from farmers, sometimes from men interested in mining rights, sometimes from men interested in coal,- and sometimes from timber men; and last, but not least, from oil prospectors. I have rereceived letters, arid I have no doubt hon. gentlemen opposite from that province have also received like letters, condemning the Government for every change and amendment they have made in the mining regulations. I have one particular letter which I will not read in full, but I may read a resolution which was passed by a meeting of citizens on this subject. The resolution is as follows:
We, therefore, submit the following resolutions :
1. There should be no Government reservations at the present time In the North West Territories. Should the Government adhere to the idea of a reserve, then the lessee should have
the prior rights to such reservations, upon payment of what royalty the Government demand.
2.	There should be no burdensome money payments required during development or before marketing of the oil becomes possible.
3.	The Government should rely mainly upon royalties for control of petroleum production, rather than upon rentals and reservations.
4.	Canada's present dependence upon foreign oil supply, and her unfavourable trade balance, suggest and require that every possible assistance and encouragement should be given to the business of developing our own oil resources.
5.	The best encouragement that the Government can offer at the present time is the adopting of a set of fixed regulations that cannot be altered except by Act of Parliament.
6.	The Government should so frame its petroleum policy as to offer every possible encouragement to foreign capital to come to, Canada.
7.	The Government would be well advised in appointing a Commission for the purpose of investigating the difficulties and practical possibilities of the MacKenzie River Basin Oil Fields; one of such Commission should be from Alberta and familiar with the geographic, climatic and transport difficulties of the North; in the interim, pending the Commission's report, the more onerous restrictions should be amended so that there will be no interference with development work going on this year.
Now let me read a further communication on this subject;
A large number of men of the city of Edmonton, who are conversant with all the development that has taken place in Western Canada, and who are looking forward anxiously to the opening up and development of Canada's * Natural Resources, beg to submit for your consideration the following observations re the issue of Oil and Gas Permits and Leases in the North-West Territories :
1.	Although capital prefers specific contracts before investment, no lease will be granted until oil has been actually found. (Section 1 and 22.)
2.	Prospecting permits cover a maximum of only four square miles, which is insufficient to warrant the heavy outlays necessary in far Northern fields. (Section 2.)
3.	Prospecting permits lapse and revert to the Government without notice upon casual or clerical defaults, and, in any event, at the end of four years, whether drilling is still proceeding or not. (Sections 16, 19 and 21.)
4.	A lease will be granted for only one-quarter of the area secured under permit. The balance becomes Crown reserve. (Section 23.)
5.	A separate drill must be set to work upon every permit acquired or held by each and every owner. This is a physical impossibility. Transportation into the North Country is limited by climatic conditions to 12 weeks. E.G., it took 27 days for the Imperial Oil, Limited, utilizing every possible resource of men and of money, at a time when there was no congestion of traffic, to transport one drill outfit over Smith Portage. (Section 15.)
6.	Rental charges must always be paid, and vigorous pumping of oil must continue at all times whether facilities for delivery of oil to a market are available or not. The only alternative is wastefully to pump into open pits. (Section 46.)
It does not matter what a man's calling may be-whether he is engaged in farm-

ing, mining, or anything else-it is difficult for him to do business in that country owing to the hampering and restrictive effect of the Government regulations.
Will the hon. gentleman give the name of the writer of the letter?
It is signed by Mr. H. L. Mclnnes, who for many years was president of the Conservative Association at Edmonton. I have no doubt my hon. friend knows him very well.

Is the
hon. gentleman aware that changes have been made in the regulations in the direction asked for?

I am very glad if that is the case. It may have the effect of awakening the Government to the necessity of making further changes in the regulations.
I now wish to draw attention to the necessity of providing adequate transportation facilities in the West. The impression exists very generally in the East that the railroads in the West were built solely for the benefit of the western people. The fact is that most of the existing roads were built before there were any settlers in the West to speak of, the number located there at that time was very few. As I said a few moments ago, as late as 1896, when a considerable number of railroads had been built, there was only one representative in this Parliament from the province of Alberta, and, I think, two from the province of Saskatchewan. These railways were built at the instance of the eastern people who should assume the responsibility therefor to as great an extent as the people of the West-western people should not be called upon to bear the entire burden. Let me point out to hon. gentlemen the extent to which increased rates on transportation facilities bears more heavily on the West than on the East. There are districts in the province of Alberta where the grain has to be marketed at a distance of approximately one thousand miles from the place of production. On the other hand, in the province of Ontario the farmer's market is not at a greater distance, probably, than fifty miles. In the West we have to pay railway rates on a thousand-mile journey, whereas in the East the railway rate only applies to a fifty-mile journey. The result of such heavy railway freight rates was demonstrated the other day by one of the members of the Agrarian party, I think the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Reid) who showed that on a

shipment of a carload of oats the producer received nothing and in addition had to pay $38 to make up the charges of the commission merchant. Whatever the reasons may be, that is the situation we are up against in the. West-we have a large crop but we have no markets for it. Does the Government think it a wise thing to maintain high railway rates and render it impossible for producers to get their products to market? Such a policy is undoubtedly limiting production and causing stagnation throughout the country. The facts in regard to the existing situation were fully placed before the Prime Minister when he visited the West last fall. I was asked to head a delegation of people from the districts along the Canadian Northern line who wished to complain to the right hon. gentleman of the existing congestion of grain and their inability to market their crop. The Prime Minister was apprised in advance that the deputation were about to wait on him, a wire beihg sent to him at Vancouver. When he met the delegation he was quite sympathetic, of course, but was unable to give any answer as to what he might be able to do. The recommendations made to the Prime Minister on that occasion were most comprehensive, the several Boards of Trade along the main line of the Canadian Northern, for a distance of one hundred miles, having drawn up statements explaining the actual conditions. No notice has been taken of those representations, although nearly a year has expired; apparently the Prime Minister has been unable to do anything. Under the circumstances I deem it well to place on Hansard the memorials addressed to the Prime Minister. By a perusal of them it may be possible to take measures to prevent a repetition of the events of last year. The first document I shall read is a memorial addressed to the Prime Minister, which reads as follows :
